questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A source base made entirely of one side's documents
questions.learningObjective: Identify a one-sided source base in a costing review
questions.stem: A chef reviews a supplier contract using only the invoices his own kitchen received, then generalises about what the dish costs across the group.

options.text: The review can only speak to what the chef's own kitchen paid, so it cannot represent the group's wider costs.
The invoices are exact, so this sample is wide enough to describe every kitchen in the group.
options.misconception: treats one kitchen's invoices as the whole group's record

options.text: The gap can be closed by averaging the invoice total with the published rate card.
options.misconception: believes a rate card replaces the missing source documents

options.text: The chef only needs more invoices from his own kitchen to make the claim general.
options.misconception: assumes more of the same source widens the sample

questions.explanation: A source base of one kitchen's invoices is one-sided by construction. A rate card and more of the same invoices leave the imbalance untouched, so a group-wide cost claim stays unsupported.
questions.hint: Ask whose documents the review never consulted.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a carried-over term leaves unsaid
questions.learningObjective: State what a carried-over term leaves unsaid
questions.stem: A menu plan calls a dish 'light' in a costing sheet, using the term from a neighbouring restaurant's menu without saying what it means there.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the term 'light' was carried over from another kitchen's menu and that its meaning there was never stated, so on this sheet it labels a dish without fixing what is to be measured. The fix is to state the measurable property the word stands for, such as grams of fat or the portion weight, before the term is used in any comparison or pricing decision.

questions.explanation: A term carried across without its definition leaves the sheet unable to say what the word denotes. Comparisons built on it then rest on an unchecked assumption, so the sheet must define the word.
questions.hint: Ask what the word was measured by in its first use.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Local categories and shared analytical terms
questions.learningObjective: Map local categories onto shared analytical terms

stimulus.body: The Copper Pot Bistro costing sheet lists 'bisque' for the roasted squash soup, 'chowder' for the cod chowder, and 'broth' for the mushroom broth. The head chef's notebook uses 'soup' for all three and adds no other categories.

questions.stem: The head chef wants the bistro's dish names mapped onto the group's shared analytical terms for the cost audit. Which step avoids losing the distinctions the local names carry?

options.text: Replace the three local names with the shared term soup so that every dish can be counted in one column.
options.misconception: assumes collapsing local names is the same as mapping them

options.text: Record each local name beside the shared term and write the rule that links them, keeping both in the sheet.
Choose the shared term for each dish only after the cost audit, so the mapping cannot bias the totals.
options.misconception: believes delayed mapping removes the need for an explicit rule

options.text: Keep the local names as decorative labels and report the shared terms to the group without linking them.
options.misconception: treats the local names as styling rather than as categories

questions.explanation: Mapping a local term onto a shared term needs the rule written down, or the shared label will be read as if it always covered the same thing. Keeping the local names visible preserves the distinctions the kitchen works with.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would have to assume without the rule.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A finding carried across a change of level
questions.learningObjective: Check whether a finding survives a change of level
questions.stem: One plate in a tasting set costs 11.40 pounds to produce and sells for 16.00 pounds, and the chef concludes that the whole tasting menu is unprofitable.

options.text: Treat the conclusion as settled, since a plate priced below cost always makes its menu unprofitable.
options.misconception: assumes the loss of one plate decides the result for the whole menu

options.text: Treat the conclusion as settled, since averaging the plate cost gives the menu its own cost per plate.
options.misconception: confuses an average of plate costs with a mix-weighted menu cost

options.text: Hold the finding at plate level, because the menu result depends on the mix of dishes and how many of each are sold.
Reject every plate-level finding, because a single dish's numbers can never say anything about a menu.
options.misconception: believes dish-level evidence is worthless for menu decisions

questions.explanation: A menu's result follows the mix of dishes and their sales shares, so a single plate's margin cannot be carried up to the menu. The plate finding stays valid, but it is evidence about one dish rather than the set.
questions.hint: Ask what else the menu figure would need to know.

questions.topic: A similarity claim contradicted by a source from inside one of the cases

questions.stem: A comparison says the bistro's braised short rib and the hotel's braised short rib behave alike, and the analyst proposes reporting the similarity as established; the bistro's own log shows 90 minutes of cooking against 4 hours at the hotel. Which sequence makes the claim defensible?

options.text: Report the similarity first, then note the cooking differences as a caveat for readers to weigh later.
options.misconception: puts the conclusion ahead of the contradicting evidence

options.text: Average the two cooking times to get a single description that covers both dishes fairly.
options.misconception: thinks a midpoint value represents both dishes

options.text: Drop the braised rib from the comparison, since a dish that differs is not comparable at all.
options.misconception: assumes any difference removes comparability

options.text: Reopen both dishes' own records, state the difference in treatment, and let it qualify how far the similarity holds.

questions.explanation: A source from inside one of the cases can qualify a similarity claim rather than destroy it, and reading it that way keeps the finding and the difference visible at once. Ignoring the record or abandoning the comparison both overstate the result.

options.text: Fix the selection criteria in writing first, so the chosen dishes reflect the contract rather than the numbers.
Choose the dishes that look most affordable once the totals arrive, so the tender can actually be won.
options.misconception: picks cases to make the outcome look good

options.text: Include every dish in the kitchen, since a larger set removes any need for selection rules.
options.misconception: believes volume of cases replaces the need for criteria

options.misconception: accepts personal recommendation as a substitute for stated criteria

questions.explanation: Criteria fixed before the results are visible protect a comparison from being tailored to the outcome, which is the whole point of setting them early. Choosing cases after seeing the totals lets the findings pick the cases.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Matching on a factor the explanation itself needs
questions.learningObjective: Match cases on a factor the explanation needs
questions.stem: A chef claims a sauce tastes better when rested longer, and the comparison lines up four sauces that also come from the same supplier, which the chef never mentions.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the comparison matches on a factor the explanation itself needs: the sauces are all bought from one supplier, so the observed difference in flavour may reflect that supplier's produce rather than the resting time. Any account that attributes the difference to resting alone has to rule out the supplier, which means either matching on it or holding it constant and recording what was held constant.

questions.explanation: If resting time is meant to explain the difference, every other thing that differs must be matched or held fixed. Leaving the supplier unmatched leaves the observed difference explainable by something the chef never named.
questions.hint: Ask what else differs between the matched sauces.

questions.topic: Two cases reporting one outcome on different definitions

stimulus.body: The bistro's costing sheet records a soup as 'prepped' once the vegetables are chopped. The hotel kitchen records the same soup as 'prepped' only after it is blended and strained.

questions.stem: The group is comparing how quickly each kitchen reaches a 'prepped' soup. What must the analyst do before the two figures can be placed on one chart?

options.text: Average the two prep times, since the word means roughly the same thing in both kitchens.
options.misconception: assumes a shared word guarantees a shared definition

options.text: State each kitchen's definition of prepped and either align them or report the figures separately.
Use the slower of the two figures for both kitchens, to keep the comparison conservative.
options.misconception: thinks one kitchen's standard can overwrite the other's

options.text: Ignore the difference, since preparation time barely affects the cost of a soup.
options.misconception: dismisses definitional drift as immaterial

questions.explanation: Two figures can sit on one chart only if they measure the same thing, and the two sheets define 'prepped' differently. Stating each definition either allows an alignment or makes separate reporting the honest option.
questions.hint: Ask what each kitchen counts as finished.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A finding carried across a change of level
questions.learningObjective: Check whether a finding survives a change of level
questions.stem: A soup is found to cost 2.80 pounds a litre in the central kitchen, and the bistro's own kitchen buys the same soup for 3.10 pounds a litre.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the finding is at the litre level in one kitchen, and the bistro's different purchase price is a separate observation rather than a refutation. The sheet can report that the two kitchens pay different prices for the same product, but it cannot turn a central-kitchen cost figure into a statement about the bistro's costs without the bistro's own purchasing evidence to stand on.

questions.explanation: A litre figure from the central kitchen describes that kitchen, while the bistro's price is evidence about the bistro. Reporting both is sound, but letting one stand in for the other is a change of level in the evidence.
questions.hint: Ask which kitchen the litre figure actually came from.

Treat the figures as the same measure, because both start from 10 kg of carrots.
options.misconception: believes a shared input makes the outputs directly comparable

options.misconception: keeps an undefined phrase because it is familiar to customers

options.text: Keep the phrase and add the supplier's full marketing line beneath it in small print.
options.misconception: hides the source definition in fine print

options.text: Keep the phrase only for the soup, where the bistro's process already matches the supplier's claim.
options.misconception: applies a phrase to one dish without checking the others

options.text: Write the operational steps the phrase commits the kitchen to and check they match before the phrase is used.

questions.explanation: A marketing phrase implies a set of operational conditions, and the only way to use it honestly is to state those conditions and check the kitchen meets them. Small print, menus alone or a single dish all leave the claim unverified.
questions.hint: Ask what the phrase would oblige the kitchen to do.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Local categories and shared analytical terms
questions.learningObjective: Map local categories onto shared analytical terms
questions.stem: A pub's sheet records 'kitchen waste' and 'bar waste' as separate lines, and the shared group category is 'front of house' for both.

options.text: Record the two local lines under the shared category with their split intact, so the pub's own figures stay readable.
Combine the two lines, because the shared category has no room for a split.
options.misconception: lets the shared form erase a distinction the local sheet keeps

options.text: Move kitchen waste into the shared food cost category, since it is a food cost.
options.misconception: reassigns a line to fit a neighbouring category

options.text: Report only bar waste, because front of house waste is what the category is about.
options.misconception: reads the category's name as its meaning

questions.explanation: The shared category can hold both local lines as long as the split between them stays visible in the record. Combining them, moving one or reporting only part of it all change what the pub's own figures say.
questions.hint: Ask what the local sheet needs to keep to stay readable.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A finding carried across a change of level
questions.learningObjective: Check whether a finding survives a change of level
questions.stem: A kitchen finds that its own waste fell from 9 per cent to 6 per cent of food spend, and a group note says 'the group has cut waste by a third'.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the reduction is real but it belongs to one kitchen, and the note has moved a site-level finding up to the group level without any evidence from the other sites. The defensible version reports the kitchen's own fall from 9 to 6 per cent, and either states a group figure only for the sites that have supplied their own numbers, or leaves the group claim out until the evidence supports it.

questions.explanation: A site-level improvement becomes a group-level claim only when the other sites' own figures support it. The number can be reported accurately at the level the evidence reaches, and no further.
questions.hint: Ask whose figures the reduction rests on.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A similarity claim contradicted by a source from inside one of the cases
questions.learningObjective: Weigh a source from inside a case against a similarity claim

stimulus.body: The bistro's recipe book shows a stew thickened with a roux of flour and butter. The group's report describes the same stew as 'thickened with a starch slurry' and cites the bistro as an example of the practice.

questions.stem: How should the report deal with the recipe book?

options.text: Keep the report as written, since flour and butter amount to a starch slurry in culinary terms.
options.misconception: equates a roux with a slurry and calls the difference semantic

options.text: Correct the description to match the recipe book, since the named technique is the substance of the example.
Remove the bistro example and cite the other kitchens, so that no description is at risk.
options.misconception: drops the case rather than correcting the record

options.text: Add a footnote that the bistro uses a roux and leave the main description unchanged.
options.misconception: buries a correction where readers will not see it

questions.explanation: The report names a technique and cites a kitchen whose own record shows a different one, so the description has to be corrected to match the source. A footnote, a swap of example or a denial all leave a false claim in circulation.
questions.hint: Ask which document the report's example comes from.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Fixing case-selection criteria before the results are seen
questions.learningObjective: Set case-selection criteria before results are seen
questions.stem: A group study of dessert plating must choose three dishes, and the analyst has already read the head chef's comments on last year's competition entries.

options.text: Choose the three dishes the head chef praised, since that person is the group's most experienced judge.
options.misconception: uses a result-adjacent source to pick the cases

options.text: Choose the three dishes the head chef criticised, so the study can measure improvement.
options.misconception: selects cases in a way that still uses the seen results

options.text: Agree the selection criteria independently of the comments and record that the comments had already been seen.
Choose the three dishes that had the most photographs, since those are the best documented.
options.misconception: treats documentation volume as a neutral selection rule

questions.explanation: Once comments are read, using them to pick the cases is selection on the outcome, even if the reason given is different. Agreeing the criteria independently and disclosing what had been seen keeps the design auditable.
questions.hint: Ask what the analyst already knew about the entries.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Matching on a factor the explanation itself needs
questions.learningObjective: Match cases on a factor the explanation needs
questions.stem: A chef says a new marinade improved grilled lamb, and the comparison sets the new marinade against the old one using lamb bought on two different days from two different butchers.

options.text: Compare the two and credit the marinade, since the marinade is the only recipe change made.
options.misconception: credits the named change while ignoring the uncontrolled ones

options.text: Compare the two and credit the marinade, since both batches were grilled by the same chef on the same grill.
options.misconception: treats a shared grill as control over the meat

options.text: Repeat the grill on a third batch of lamb to see whether the difference persists.
options.misconception: adds another unmatchable batch to the comparison

options.text: Buy lamb from one butcher for both batches, hold the grilling identical and vary only the marinade.

questions.explanation: The marinade can only be credited with the improvement if the meat is the same, so both batches have to come from one butcher. A third batch or a shared grill adds no control over the factor that actually differs.
questions.hint: Ask where the two batches of lamb came from.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Two cases reporting one outcome on different definitions
questions.learningObjective: Separate outcomes measured on different definitions
questions.stem: A cafe reports an 'average ticket' of 11.40 pounds and a bistro reports an 'average spend per cover' of 13.90 pounds, and the group compares the two on one chart.

options.text: Treat the two as different measures until their components are set out, since a ticket and a spend per cover are not defined alike.
Treat the two as the same measure, because both divide money taken by the number of people served.
options.misconception: assumes a shared divisor makes two measures identical

options.text: Treat the two as the same measure, because both are quoted per customer in pounds.
options.misconception: treats shared units as shared definitions

options.text: Treat the two as the same measure, because a ticket always equals a cover's spend in a small room.
options.misconception: relies on an accident of room size as a rule

questions.explanation: A ticket and a spend per cover can be built from different components, and shared units or a shared divisor do not fix that. Until the components are set out, the two figures are different measures sitting on the same chart.
questions.hint: Ask what goes into each figure before it is divided.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A source base made entirely of one side's documents
questions.learningObjective: Identify a one-sided source base in a costing review
questions.stem: A tender report claims the group understands its own supply chain better than any rival, on the strength of the group's internal cost sheets alone.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the claim is a comparison with rivals, so evidence drawn only from the group's own files cannot establish it, however detailed those files are. The internal sheets show what the group knows about itself; to support a claim about rivals' understanding, the report would need sources that reach the rivals' own records, or it has to drop the comparative claim and present only what the group's own evidence shows.

questions.explanation: A claim about how the group compares with rivals needs sources that reach the rivals, and internal files cannot reach them. The internal evidence can support a claim about the group, but not a comparative one.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the comparison the sources reach.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a carried-over term leaves unsaid
questions.learningObjective: State what a carried-over term leaves unsaid

stimulus.body: A costing sheet from the group says a dish is 'seasonal'. The bistro's head chef explains that the kitchen means dishes that use whatever is at its best that week, including herbs from a garden supplier.

questions.stem: What does the group's word 'seasonal' leave unsaid in the bistro's sheet?

options.text: Nothing, because seasonal food is a clear idea that needs no further definition.
options.misconception: treats a familiar word as self-defining

options.text: It leaves unsaid which produce counts as seasonal for this kitchen and on whose judgement that rests.
It leaves unsaid how the dishes are priced, since seasonal items change price by the week.
options.misconception: redirects the gap to pricing rather than to meaning

options.text: It leaves unsaid which of the bistro's customers value seasonal cooking most.
options.misconception: turns a definitional gap into a question about customers

questions.explanation: The word is carried over as a label and the sheet never says what qualifies a dish under it, so the qualifying judgement is left invisible. Pricing is a downstream consequence, and the customers are not part of the definition at all.
questions.hint: Ask who decides what counts as seasonal here.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Local categories and shared analytical terms
questions.learningObjective: Map local categories onto shared analytical terms
questions.stem: A school kitchen's sheet uses 'packed lunch' for a meal box and a 'set meal' for a plated service, and the shared group analysis has one 'meal' category for both.

options.text: Map both to the shared category, because the shared analysis has no alternative term available.
options.misconception: assumes a shared category fits any local term

options.text: Map only the packed lunch and leave the plated service out of the group analysis entirely.
options.misconception: drops a case to avoid a mapping decision

options.text: Map both, record which local line each covers and report the school's meal counts with the breakdown.
Rename the two local lines to the shared term on the school's sheet before the analysis begins.
options.misconception: rewrites the record to remove the difference from view

questions.explanation: The shared category can cover both local lines provided the mapping and the split are recorded, so the group's figure is usable and still honest. Renaming the source record hides the difference instead of explaining it.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader needs alongside the shared total.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A finding carried across a change of level
questions.learningObjective: Check whether a finding survives a change of level
questions.stem: A stock count finds 14 kg of chickpeas in the bistro's dry store, and the group intends to announce a group-wide stock position from this figure.

options.text: Announce 14 kg, since a stock position is a stock position wherever it happens to be counted.
options.misconception: treats a single site's count as a group total

options.text: Announce 14 kg multiplied by the number of sites, as a reasonable estimate of the group's stock.
options.misconception: extrapolates a count across sites with no basis

options.text: Announce nothing, since stock counts are too small a measure to report to the group.
options.misconception: dismisses a valid measure because of its size

options.text: Report the bistro's own count, and treat any group figure as needing the other kitchens' own counts first.

questions.explanation: A stock count is a valid measure of one store, so it should be reported, but it cannot be scaled into a group position without the other stores' counts. The rule is to report at the level the evidence reaches and no further.
questions.hint: Ask whose shelves the count covered.
